message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated this number – now called the **Shannon number** – to be on the order of

\[
\boxed{10^{43}\text{ possible positions}}
\]

This figure is an estimate; more recent computational work has refined it to roughly \(10^{46}\)–\(10^{47}\) legal positions, but the consensus is that the true count lies somewhere in the \(10^{43}\)–\(10^{47}\) range.

For comparison, the number of possible *games* (i.e., sequences of legal moves from the starting position) is even larger—often quoted as about \(10^{120}\).  But when people ask for “the total number of possible arrangements” in chess, they’re almost always referring to the Shannon number, i.e., the count of distinct board positions.
